voyage: Battery C's embarkation roster of 17 Jul (p0561-p0564). The report of 18 Jul has the battery aboard; on 19 Jul it is at Gela, a week after the first landings there (10 Jul).
about: A US Navy tank landing ship (LST-1 class), built by Bethlehem Steel at Quincy, Mass., and commissioned on 23 Jan 1943. She took part in the Sicily landings (July 1943), Salerno (September 1943) and Normandy (June 1944), and earned three battle stars. Scrapped 1947.

voyage: 9 Aug 1944, 1200: "4 Officers, 87 EM Boarded LST 318, 2 Officer 31 EM Boarded LST 313" in Naples harbour (p1143). 12 Aug: "1630 hrs left Naples Harbor, Mission Unknown" (p1146). 15 Aug: landed near Sainte-Maxime; the battalion's first tracks were on the beach at about 1030 and everything was ashore by 1400 (battalion history, ok45th-17564/p05). Most of the forward detachment was on 318.
about: Not the US Navy's LST-318, which was sunk by German aircraft off Caronia, Sicily, on 9 Aug 1943. The number the clerk typed (twice, on 9 and 12 Aug) may be a serial in the landing's loading plan rather than a hull number, or mistyped. Which ship it was isn't known.

voyage: 2 officers and 31 men of the forward detachment boarded "LST 313" (p1143).
about: Not the US Navy's LST-313, which was sunk by German aircraft off Gela on 10 Jul 1943. As with 318, the number may be a loading serial or mistyped; the ship isn't known.

voyage: 16 Oct 1943: the detachment's station is "Ship # 416" (p0622), after the Bizerte staging area, its station since 1 Oct. 17 Oct: Agnano racecourse, Naples (p0624).
about: The report gives no type. One candidate is HM LST-416, an American-built tank landing ship (Bethlehem-Fairfield, Baltimore) commissioned into the Royal Navy on 3 Feb 1943, but no source found puts her on the Bizerte-Naples run that October. Unconfirmed.

voyage: 1 Sep 1944: "Two Officers & 5 EM Relvd Fr rations Hq & Hq Btry to Det for rations to the U.S.S. Florence Nightingale (1230)" (p0668). By 4 Sep the detachment was ashore at Cogolin. Its last station before was Qualiano, near Naples (21 Aug); the navy history describes her reinforcement voyages to southern France as from Oran, so where she took the detachment aboard isn't settled.
about: A US Navy transport (Elizabeth C. Stanton class), launched in 1940 at Oakland, Calif., as the freighter Mormacsun; 492 ft, 18 knots. She landed troops at Port Lyautey, Morocco (Nov 1942) and Scoglitti, Sicily (Jul 1943), sortied from Naples for the 15 Aug 1944 assault on southern France, and carried reinforcements there until 25 Oct. Later in the Pacific (Okinawa, May 1945). Four battle stars.

voyage: Embarked at Glasgow 22 Dec 1942 at 1500 (p0397); sailed in convoy 26 Dec 0030; arrived at Algiers at 1500 on one of 1-3 Jan 1943, disembarked 1700 (p0412, "Stathaird" there).
about: The P&O liner Strathaird (1932), a troopship from 1940.

voyage: Bizerte to Sicily: aboard 22-23 Jul (p0746-p0749); "South of Empedocle, Sicily" on 24 Jul (p0750).
about: A US Navy tank landing ship, laid down 7 Sep 1942 at the New York Navy Yard and commissioned 15 Jan 1943; Sicily (July 1943), Salerno and Normandy, where a torpedo sank her on 9 Jun 1944. Three battle stars (DANFS).

voyage: Bizerte to Sicily: aboard 21 Jul (p0536), "At Sea" 22 Jul (p0537); Licata 23 Jul (p0539).
about: A US Navy tank landing ship, laid down 9 Nov 1942 at the Norfolk Navy Yard and commissioned 26 Feb 1943; Sicily (July 1943), Salerno, Anzio-Nettuno, Elba and Pianosa, and southern France; transferred to the United Kingdom 24 Dec 1944, returned 1946 and sold to Greece. Four battle stars (DANFS).

voyage: Boarded at 1630 on 28 Aug at the 57th St pier, New York (p0372); sailed 1005 on 31 Aug "Aboard HMS Queen Elizabeth"; at sea 1-4 Sep "aboard HMT Queen Elizabeth" (p0389); anchored at Greenock 1900 on 5 Sep (p0389).
about: The Cunard liner (launched 1938 at Clydebank), the largest passenger ship then built; a troopship from 1940, painted grey, sailing fast and usually alone across the Atlantic (Wikipedia).

voyage: "AT SEA ABROAD TRANSPORT NY 400" (as read) 1-4 Sep; anchored at Greenock 1700 on 5 Sep (p0502). The ship is not named. Battery C of the same battalion crossed in the Queen Elizabeth on the same days, anchoring at Greenock the same evening (rg64-427182819/p0389), so probably the same ship (inferred); "NY 400" may be a transport or troop-movement number.
about: The Cunard liner (launched 1938 at Clydebank), the largest passenger ship then built; a troopship from 1940, painted grey, sailing fast and usually alone across the Atlantic (Wikipedia).

voyage: Detrained at Gourock 1355 on 29 Oct and boarded ship; 30-31 Oct "Usual duties aboard ship USAT Argentina" (p0405); sailed 1 Nov and arrived at Mers El Kébir 11 Nov (convoy KMF 2, inferred; routes.csv).
about: The Moore-McCormack liner (built 1929 as the Pennsylvania, renamed 1938), requisitioned in January 1942 as a US Army transport; she had already landed troops at Gourock in July 1942, and later sailed to Casablanca (December 1942) and Cherbourg (1944) (Wikipedia, which does not list this Oct-Nov 1942 voyage).

voyage: "Detrained GUROCK ENG 14:30, embarked on SHIP ARGENTINA 1740" (p0519); sailed from Gourock 1 Nov and arrived at Mers-el-Kébir 11 Nov (p0535).
about: The Moore-McCormack liner (built 1929 as the Pennsylvania, renamed 1938), requisitioned in January 1942 as a US Army transport; she had already landed troops at Gourock in July 1942, and later sailed to Casablanca (December 1942) and Cherbourg (1944) (Wikipedia, which does not list this Oct-Nov 1942 voyage).

voyage: "At sea on U.S.S. Anacon" (p0058; as written). The Regimental HQ Battery's report has the regiment leaving Fort Dix by rail on 13 Jan and embarking at the New York Port of Embarkation; convoy UGF-4; disembarked at Mers-el-Kébir 26 Jan (p0058).
about: The Panama Railroad Company liner (launched 1938), an Army transport from January 1942 and in Navy commission from August 1942 as USS Ancon (AP-66); flagship of a transport division at Fedhala in Operation Torch; she sailed for Algeria on 14 Jan 1943 and reached Oran on the 26th (Wikipedia; later the headquarters ship AGC-4).
